physical_harm: Injuries and death caused by burning with kerosene
number_of_offences: Multiple charges under Sections 376, 302, 201 and 506 IPC; all upheld
premeditation_planning: Yes, the court found premeditation and planning to cause disappearance of evidence and screen the offence
key_evidence_accepted: The extra-judicial confession made by the appellant to PW-2 was accepted by the trial court and the High Court as it was within the parameters of law and withstood the test of reasonableness and credibility. The evidence of PWs 2 & 3, along with the post-mortem certificate and the reports of scientific officers, established the case of murder beyond doubt.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of PW-2 as reliable, noting that her statement corroborated with the confession of the accused and the evidence of PW-1 and PW-3. The court found no reason to disbelieve her testimony and accepted her evidence as acceptable when considered with other circumstances.

legal_representation.accused: V. Krishnamurthy, Prasanth P., V. Vasudevan, T. Harish Kumar, K.V. Bharathi Upadhyaya
legal_representation.state: Subramonium Prasad, AAG, M. Yogesh Kanna, A. Santha Kumaran, Sasikala

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant-accused intended to rape his sister-in-law, and after she resisted, he struck her with 'poorikatai' causing her unconsciousness, then had sexual intercourse with her. He then attacked her 13-month-old daughter, causing her unconsciousness as well. The appellant-accused then caused the death of his sister-in-law and her daughter by pouring kerosene and setting them on fire. The prosecution also proved the motive, the threat to PW-2, and the impersonation of the deceased to make it appear as a suicidal case. The evidence of PWs 1, 2, and 3, along with the post-mortem report and scientific reports, established the case of murder.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the conviction solely based on the extra-judicial confession made to PW-2 was not sustainable as she did not disclose the incident at the earliest. They also contended that the complaint (Exh. P-1) did not mention the accused's conduct towards the deceased, PW-3's evidence was inconsistent, and the evidence did not prove the offence under Sections 376, 302, and 201 IPC with medical evidence beyond reasonable doubt.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that if an extra-judicial confession is voluntary and made in a fit state of mind, it can be relied upon along with other materials. The Court also emphasized the proportionality between the rigor of the offence and the penalty imposed, and the need for exemplary treatment for crimes against women.
precedent_relied_upon: Swami Shraddananda (2) @ Murli Manohar Mishra vs. State of Karnataka (2008) 13 SCC 767 and Sahib Hussain @ Sahib Jan vs. State of Rajasthan 2013 (6) SCALE 219
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence of life imprisonment was imposed due to the heinous nature of the crime, which included rape followed by double murder. The Court emphasized the need for exemplary treatment for crimes against women and the public abhorrence of such crimes.
